t: #4021 Minimum Operations to Make a Rotated Palindrome I — Rotation Enumeration with Circular Pair Costs
o:
## Understanding the problem
You may left-rotate the string (cost 1 per rotation) and increment characters cyclically ('z'->'a', cost 1 per step). Minimize total operations to reach a palindrome.

Example 1 `"abc"`: rotate once to `"bca"`, then bump 'a' to 'b' (1 op) — total 2. Example 2 `"yb"`: no rotation helps enough; raising 'y' three times to 'b' gives `"bb"` — total 3.

With n <= 2000, trying all n rotations and fixing each candidate in O(n) gives O(n^2) = 4·10^6 operations — perfectly fine, so no fancy algorithm is required. The key detail is that increments only go forward but wrap around, so aligning a pair costs `min((x-y) mod 26, (y-x) mod 26)`.
k: There are only n distinct rotations; evaluating each independently is O(n^2) total, well within limits.
To equalize a mirrored pair with circular increments, the cheapest cost is the circular letter distance between the two characters.
The middle character of an odd-length string never needs changes.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate all rotations, fix pairs greedily
a.i: For each rotation count r, form the rotated string and compute the cost to make it a palindrome: for each mirrored pair, add the circular distance between the two letters. Add r for the rotations themselves and take the global minimum. Greedy per-pair alignment is optimal because pairs are independent.
s: For r = 0..n-1, build t = s[r:] + s[:r].
Cost = r + sum over i < n/2 of circular distance between t[i] and t[n-1-i].
Return the minimum cost over all r.
a.t: O(n^2) — n rotations, each scanned in O(n); with early breaking when the running cost exceeds the best.
a.sp: O(n) for each rotated copy of the string.

w:
## Wrap-up
This single approach is the intended solution — the constraints (n <= 2000) are sized exactly for O(n^2) rotation enumeration, and there is no meaningfully faster standard technique because the per-pair `min` over two directions blocks linear sliding-window tricks. Common pitfalls: treating increments as bidirectional absolute differences (they wrap 'z'->'a'), forgetting to add the rotation count r, and mishandling odd-length strings (skip the middle character). Follow-ups: what if decrements were also allowed (cost becomes plain circular distance either way — same formula), or if rotations cost differently in each direction?
